lessons.title: Where AI is already around you

tasks.question: Which of these uses AI?
hints: Think about which of these adapts to you personally.
Which system “learns” from what you watch and like?
tasks.explanation: Recommendations are picked by AI: it analyzes what you watch and suggests similar things. A calculator just follows fixed rules — it doesn’t learn.

tasks.question: A voice assistant followed the command “Play music”. What did it do?
options: Turned speech into text and recognized the command
hints: The assistant can’t see you — it only hears sound.
First the sound has to become something a program can work with.
tasks.explanation: A voice assistant first recognizes speech and turns it into text, then AI understands the meaning of the command. No magic, no mind reading.

tasks.question: Why does a social media filter sometimes work badly on some faces?
options: AI learned from examples with few faces like that
hints: Remember: AI learns from examples. What if there are few examples?
If some faces were almost missing in training, AI “doesn’t know” how to handle them.
tasks.explanation: AI learns from data. If the data had few examples of certain faces, AI makes mistakes exactly on them. That’s why developers need diverse data.

tasks.question: AI confidently named a book that doesn’t exist. What is this called?
hints: It’s a special word for when AI confidently makes up facts.
The word is usually about “seeing” something that isn’t there.
tasks.explanation: When AI confidently invents facts, books or links, it’s called a hallucination. That’s why important facts always need checking.

tasks.question: AI said: “The Great Wall of China is visible from space with the naked eye.” Is that true?
options: Sounds right, no need to check
hints: “Everyone knows” doesn’t mean “checked”. What do astronauts say?
The wall is long but narrow — a few meters. Could you see something as wide as a road from 400 km?
tasks.explanation: It’s a popular myth. Astronauts, including Yang Liwei — China’s first astronaut, said they could not see the wall from orbit with the naked eye. AI repeated a common mistake.

tasks.question: AI named the winner of an important match last week. What’s the most reliable way to check?
options: Find the official website or news from at least two sources
Believe it if the answer is long and detailed
hints: AI may not know recent events. Where are match results published?
Reliable checking means independent sources, not the same AI.
tasks.explanation: AI may not know recent events or may mix them up. The most reliable check is an official source or news from two different places. Asking the same AI “are you sure?” proves nothing.

tasks.question: You were asked to make a presentation. Which question helps you understand the task best?
options: “Who will watch it and what should they understand?”
hints: A good question clarifies the goal, not design details.
Think about the people the presentation is for.
tasks.explanation: Understanding the audience and the goal is the basis of any task. Fonts and design matter, but only after you know why and for whom you’re working.

tasks.question: A friend says: “I’m bored in class.” Which question is best to ask first?
options: “In which classes and at what moments are you bored?”
hints: First understand the problem, don’t solve it or argue.
A good question clarifies: where, when, why.
tasks.explanation: A clarifying question helps you find the real cause. Maybe it’s only one subject, or only when everything is already clear. The solution comes later.

tasks.question: Your team is arguing about which game to make for a contest. What’s the best way to decide?
options: Pick the idea of whoever is loudest
Write down criteria (time, interest, difficulty) and compare ideas
Ask AI to choose for everyone
hints: A good decision can be explained, not just “it happened”.
Try judging all ideas by the same rules.
tasks.explanation: Criteria make a decision fair and clear for the whole team. AI can help compare ideas, but choosing and owning the decision is up to you.

tasks.question: Which approach helps you come up with more ideas?
options: Pick the first idea right away
Write down 10 ideas without judging, then choose
hints: Judging too early “kills” new ideas.
Quantity first, quality later.
tasks.explanation: First write everything down without judging — that’s how unexpected ideas appear. Choosing and improving works better as a second step.

tasks.question: AI suggested 20 ideas for a school project. What next?
options: Rate the ideas by criteria and develop the best one in your own words
hints: Lots of ideas is only the start of the work.
What makes an idea truly yours?
tasks.explanation: AI is good at generating options; people are good at choosing and refining. Rate the ideas, pick the best one and make it yours: add your own experience and interests.

tasks.question: You made a poster, but your classmates didn’t get it. What’s the best next step?
options: Decide they just don’t get it
Ask what was unclear and improve the poster
Make the font bigger without asking anyone
hints: Feedback is a hint, not an insult.
To fix it, you first need to know what exactly is wrong.
tasks.explanation: Feedback helps improve your work. First find out what exactly is unclear, then fix it. Designers and developers work the same way: try → get feedback → improve.

tasks.question: What matters most to add to the request “Make a workout plan”?
options: Context: age, goal and how much time you have
Nothing, AI will figure it out
hints: AI knows nothing about you until you tell it.
A plan for a pro athlete and for a 12-year-old beginner is different.
tasks.explanation: Context is the most important part of a request. Without it AI gives a generic answer. With your age, goal and time, the plan will fit you.

tasks.question: Which request is best if you need to understand photosynthesis?
options: “Explain it like to a biology professor”
“Explain photosynthesis to a 6th grader in 5 sentences with a real-life example”
hints: A good request says who the answer is for and how long it should be.
Find the option with an audience, a length and an example.
tasks.explanation: A good request has a topic, an audience, a length and a format. The answer will be clear and not too long.

tasks.question: You’re doing an ecology project with AI. How should you organize the work?
options: Break it into steps: ideas → plan → text → fact-check
Ask AI to do the whole project at once
hints: A big task is easier to solve in parts.
At which step do you check that AI didn’t make mistakes?
tasks.explanation: A complex task is better broken into steps. At every step you control the result, and at the end you check the facts. The project stays yours, and AI is the helper.

tasks.question: AI gave an answer that’s too complicated. What’s best to write?
options: “Explain it more simply, like to an 11-year-old, with an example”
hints: AI doesn’t know the answer didn’t work for you until you say why.
Say what the answer should be like.
tasks.explanation: Talking to AI is a dialogue. If an answer didn’t work, explain what to change: simpler, shorter, with an example. The second answer is usually much better.

tasks.question: You need a name for a school blog. Which request is better?
options: “Suggest 5 different names for a science blog for teens and explain the pros of each”
hints: Several options beat one: you have something to choose from.
A good request explains what the blog is about and who it’s for.
tasks.explanation: Asking for several options with explanations gives you a choice and shows how they differ. The decision stays with you.

tasks.question: AI wrote a story, but the ending is boring. Which request is best?
options: “Keep the beginning, rewrite only the ending: a surprising twist, 5 sentences, a happy finish”
hints: No need to rewrite everything if only one part is bad.
Say exactly what to keep, what to change and what the result should be.
tasks.explanation: The best improvement request says what to keep, what to change and what result you need. That way AI won’t spoil what already works.

games.name: Games & tech
games.desc: How AI controls characters and helps make games

tasks.question: Enemies in a game walk around obstacles and look for you. Who controls them?
options: Game AI — a program that chooses actions
hints: Enemies act just as smart even when you play alone.
There’s a program inside the game that decides where an enemy goes.
tasks.explanation: Enemies are controlled by game AI: a program that follows rules to choose where to go and what to do. That’s why enemies seem “smart” even when you play alone.

tasks.question: An AI learned to beat a level: it tried thousands of times and got points for success. What is this called?
hints: Think about how a dog is trained: a reward for the right action.
The name includes a word about rewards and support.
tasks.explanation: This is reinforcement learning: AI tries different actions and gets a “reward” for good ones. Over time it picks what earns more points.

tasks.question: The AI opponent always wins and the game gets boring. What should the developer do?
options: Remove the AI from the game
Adjust the difficulty to the player’s level
hints: A game is fun when winning is possible but not too easy.
Good games adapt to whoever is playing.
tasks.explanation: The best games adjust difficulty to the player: easier for beginners, harder for pros. AI can be tuned to be a fun opponent rather than an unbeatable one.

tasks.question: You’re creating a game character with AI. Which request is better?
options: “Invent a kind robot chef for a kitchen game: name, personality and one superpower”
hints: AI doesn’t know your game until you tell it.
The best request says who the character is and what to come up with.
tasks.explanation: The more detailed the request, the more interesting the result: the game’s theme, the personality and exactly what to invent. Then you pick and polish the idea.

tasks.question: AI wrote the rules for your game, but they contradict each other. What should you do?
options: Ask AI to find and fix the contradiction, then check it yourself
hints: A mistake can be fixed — no need to drop all the work.
AI can help fix it, but you should check the result.
tasks.explanation: AI can make mistakes in game rules too. Ask it to find the contradiction, but always check the result yourself — for example, play a test round with friends.

tasks.question: You’re making a game with AI. Which order of work is best?
options: Idea → rules → simple prototype → test with friends → improve
Ask AI to do everything for you
hints: First you need to know what the game even is.
At which step do you find out whether people enjoy it?
tasks.explanation: That’s how real developers work: idea, rules, quick prototype, test and improve. AI helps at every step, but you make the decisions.

creative.name: Creativity
creative.desc: Drawings, music, videos and stories with AI

tasks.question: AI drew a picture from your description. Whose idea was it?
hints: How did AI know what exactly to draw?
Without your description there would be no picture.
tasks.explanation: The idea is yours: you described what you wanted to see. AI was a tool, like a brush or a pencil — just a very fast one.

tasks.question: How can you make an AI picture closer to what you imagine?
options: Describe the style, colors, mood and details
hints: AI can’t see the picture in your head.
The more details you describe, the more accurate the result.
tasks.explanation: AI draws what it understood from the description. Style (cartoon, watercolor), colors, mood and details help it match your idea.

tasks.question: You made a picture with AI for a drawing contest. What’s the honest thing to do?
options: Say you used AI and explain what you did yourself
Present the work as entirely yours
Change the colors a bit so you don’t have to say
hints: Think whether it’s fair to those who drew by hand.
Honesty means saying which part is yours and which is AI’s.
tasks.explanation: The honest way is to say you used AI and explain your part: the idea, the description, the edits. Many contests have special rules for this.

tasks.question: AI helped you come up with a melody. What’s still your job?
options: Pick what sounds good and add your own ideas
hints: Who decides whether you like the melody?
AI suggests options — a person chooses and improves.
tasks.explanation: AI can suggest melodies, but the taste is yours. You pick the best, change it and add your ideas — that’s how it becomes your music.

tasks.question: You’re filming a video for your blog. Where will AI help the most?
options: Make subtitles and suggest title ideas
Watch the video instead of your viewers
hints: Viewers are interested in you — what can you hand to a helper?
Think about boring but useful work.
tasks.explanation: AI is great at routine work: subtitles, title ideas, editing tips. The story, emotions and personality are why people watch you.

tasks.question: AI wrote a video script, but it doesn’t sound “like you”. Best next step?
options: Give AI examples of your phrases, ask it to rewrite in your style, then edit it yourself
Ask a friend to voice it instead of you
hints: AI doesn’t know how you usually talk.
Show AI your style, and make the final version yourself.
tasks.explanation: You can “tune” AI to your style by showing it examples. But you have the final word: edit the text so it sounds natural.

science.name: Science & nature
science.desc: Space, animals and experiments with AI

tasks.question: Scientists use AI to find new planets in telescope images. Why is AI useful?
options: It quickly scans millions of images
hints: There are so many images a person couldn’t look through them in a lifetime.
AI shines when huge amounts of data need to be processed fast.
tasks.explanation: AI quickly finds what might be a planet among millions of images. Then scientists check the most interesting finds.

tasks.question: AI identified a bird species from a photo. How can you check if it’s right?
options: Compare with a bird guide or ask an expert
hints: You need an independent source, not the same AI.
Where are verified bird descriptions collected?
tasks.explanation: AI can mix up similar species. The reliable way is to compare with a field guide or encyclopedia, or ask a bird expert. Real scientists do the same.

tasks.question: An AI weather forecast says: “80% chance of rain tomorrow.” What does it mean?
options: Rain is very likely but not guaranteed
hints: Imagine 10 similar days: on how many of them would it rain?
tasks.explanation: An 80% chance means that on about 8 out of 10 similar days it rained. It probably will — better take an umbrella — but there’s no guarantee. AI talks about chances, not the exact future.

tasks.question: You want to know why leaves turn yellow in autumn. What’s the best way to ask AI?
options: “Explain in simple words why leaves turn yellow in autumn and give an example”
hints: One word isn’t a question.
A good question says what you want to know and how to explain it.
tasks.explanation: A full question asking for a simple explanation gets a clear answer. In short: in autumn the green chlorophyll in leaves breaks down and the yellow pigments show.

tasks.question: AI wrote in your report: “Whales are big fish.” What will you do?
options: Check it: whales are mammals, so AI was wrong
Copy it into the report as is
Ask AI “really?” and trust the answer
hints: Remember: how do whales breathe and feed their babies?
Whales breathe air and feed their babies milk.
tasks.explanation: Whales are mammals: they breathe air and feed their babies milk. AI got it wrong, so facts for a report always need checking in a textbook or encyclopedia.

tasks.question: You’re doing a school project on how clean a river’s water is. How should you use AI?
options: Collect your own data and ask AI to help analyze and present it
Ask AI to invent the measurement results
hints: A science project is built on real data.
AI can help with analysis, but shouldn’t invent facts.
tasks.explanation: Real science means real data. Take your own measurements, and use AI to build a chart, find patterns and present your conclusions nicely.

sport.name: Sport & health
sport.desc: Smartwatches, match analysis and training with AI

tasks.question: A smartwatch counts your steps and heart rate. What does AI do with this data?
hints: Why does a watch need so many numbers about you?
For example, the watch can notice you haven’t moved much today.
tasks.explanation: AI finds patterns in the data: how much you move, how you sleep, how your heart rate changes — and suggests what to improve.

tasks.question: A football club analyzes matches with AI. What can AI find?
options: Which players lose the ball most often and in which zone
Who is the best friend on the team
hints: AI analyzes what already happened in matches.
Look for an answer that can be counted from game recordings.
tasks.explanation: AI finds patterns in match recordings: where the ball is lost, where goals come from. This helps the coach, but AI can’t count the future or friendship.

tasks.question: An AI coach advises a 12-year-old to train 5 hours every day. What should you do?
options: Obey the AI — it’s the coach
Talk to an adult coach or doctor — the AI may have ignored your age
hints: That schedule is hard even for adult athletes.
When it comes to health, an adult specialist has the final word.
tasks.explanation: AI can give unsuitable advice, especially if it doesn’t know your age and health. On health questions, always check with a coach, a doctor or your parents.

tasks.question: Which request will give a useful warm-up plan?
options: “Make a 10-minute warm-up before football for a 6th grader”
hints: AI needs to know which sport and who the warm-up is for.
Find the request with time, sport and age.
tasks.explanation: A good request includes the time, the sport and the age. Then the warm-up will be suitable and safe for you.

tasks.question: An AI app says you ran 50 km in 10 minutes. What’s wrong?
options: Nobody can run that fast — the data is wrong, check the sensor
hints: Compare with a car: how far does it go in 10 minutes in a city?
If a result is impossible, the data is wrong.
tasks.explanation: 50 km in 10 minutes is the speed of a car on a highway. The AI calculated from bad sensor data. If a result looks impossible — check the data.

tasks.question: A team wants to use AI to choose tactics for a match. Who makes the decision?
options: The coach and the team, while AI provides ideas and stats
hints: AI doesn’t know the team’s mood or who is in shape today.
AI is a helper; a person is responsible for the decision.
tasks.explanation: AI is good at stats and suggesting options, but the coach and players decide: they know the team, the opponent and the situation on the pitch.
